en: Title: Lokātītastava Author: Nāgārjuna Source:
Tola & Dragonetti, 1985, pp. 10–12; to be compared with the edition by Tsuda and the forthcoming edition by Choezom.
Homage to you, Lokātīta, who perceive through isolated gnosis.
You, who out of compassion have long been weary for the sake of the world’s welfare—
though it is your view that no sentient being exists apart from the mere aggregate of the constituents—
you nevertheless underwent supreme exhaustion for the benefit of sentient beings, O Great Sage.
O wise one, you have also fully revealed to the wise those aggregates as being like an illusion,
a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, and a dream; for they arise from causes, and in the absence of those [causes], they do not exist.
How indeed could they not be clearly considered like reflections?
(4) The elements are not graspable by the eye; how then can that which consists of them be visual?
By speaking thus, you yourself have refuted the grasping of form. (5)
Without that which is to be felt, there is no feeling; therefore, it is devoid of self. And you maintain that this object of feeling does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature.
If the designation and the object were non-different, then one's mouth would be burned by fire.
"O speaker of truth, you have stated that if there were otherness [between agent and action], there would be no realization [of the act].
You have also stated, from the perspective of conventional usage, that the agent is independent and so too is the action;
yet, you maintain that the establishment of these two is mutually dependent."
There is no agent, nor is there an enjoyer; merit and demerit are born dependently.
O Vācaspati, you have declared that whatever is dependently arisen has not [inherently] been born.
That which is unknown is not an object of knowledge, and without it, there is no consciousness.

Therefore, you have stated that knowledge and the object of knowledge do not exist by way of intrinsic nature. (10) If the characteristic were different from the characterized, then that characterized would be without characteristics.
You have clearly stated that if they were non-different, both would be non-existent. (11)
This world has been seen by you with the eye of knowledge as peaceful, free from the characterized and the characteristic, and devoid of verbal expression.
An entity does not arise as existent, nor as non-existent, nor as both existent and non-existent.
How could it be born from itself, nor from another, nor from both?

(13) The destruction of that which exists and is endowed with stability is not possible; nor is there [destruction] of that which does not exist, for how could there be cessation of that which is like a horse’s horn? (14)
Destruction is considered to be neither a different entity from the thing nor a non-different entity.
If it were a different entity, the thing would be eternal; if it were a non-different entity, it could not occur [as destruction].
For if there were identity, the destruction of the thing would be logically impossible.
For the destruction of an entity is not tenable if it exists as something separate [from itself].

First of all, the arising of an effect from a cause that has already perished is not logical; nor is the arising from a cause that has not perished tenable, for you consider such arising to be like a dream.
The sprout does not arise from a seed that has ceased, nor from one that has not ceased;
indeed, you declare that all arising is like the arising of an illusion.
Therefore, you [teach] that this world arises from conceptual construction.
That which is unreal has been fully understood; it is unarisen and does not perish.
There is no transmigration for the eternal, nor is there transmigration for the impermanent.
Transmigration has been described by you, O best among the knowers of reality, as being like a dream. (19–20)
Logicians maintain that suffering is self-caused, caused by another, caused by both, or without cause; but you have stated that it arises dependently.
That which is dependent origination is, in your view, itself emptiness.
"There is no independent entity"—this is your peerless lion’s roar.
You have taught the nectar of emptiness for the sake of destroying all conceptual constructions;
yet, whoever clings even to that, they have been brought to ruin by you.

O Protector, you have revealed that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature— inactive, powerless, empty, and arisen from conditions like an illusion. Nothing whatsoever has been produced by you, nor has anything whatsoever been ceased.
Just as it was before, so you have awakened to suchness afterward; for indeed,
without having relied upon this cultivation practiced by the noble ones.
For consciousness does not exist here in any way whatsoever without a sign (animitta).
You have stated that there is no liberation without having attained the signless;
therefore, you have taught that [signlessness] in its entirety within the Mahāyāna.
By whatever merit I have acquired through praising you, the worthy object of praise, may the entire world thereby be freed from the bondage of causal signs. 28
